source_refs.note: Topic 14.6 (PDF 31, printed 28) as printed: Eqs 14.19-14.21 with Fig. 14.9 (a, b, c) and the phase statements.

blocks.text: The graphical representations of displacement, velocity and acceleration of a body executing SHM is given in Fig. 14.9 (a, b and c).
(i) The displacement of the particle executing SHM is given by the expression:
This shows that the particle will have maximum displacement (x₀) at extreme position.

blocks.alt: Graph of displacement against time over one period, with dashed lines at each quarter period and at xo and -xo. The curve starts at +xo, falls through zero to -xo and rises back to +xo.
blocks.caption: Figure 14.9 (a): Graphical representation of displacement of oscillation performing S.H.M (original drawing after the textbook's Figure 14.9 (a)).

blocks.text: (ii) The velocity of the particle executing SHM is given by the expression:
The velocity of the particle is maximum (i.e., v = x₀ω) at the mean position and zero at the extreme positions.

blocks.alt: Graph of velocity against time over one period, between xo omega and -xo omega. The curve starts at zero, falls to -xo omega after a quarter period, crosses zero at half a period, reaches +xo omega at three quarters and returns to zero.
blocks.caption: Figure 14.9 (b): Graphical representation of velocity of oscillation performing S.H.M (original drawing after the textbook's Figure 14.9 (b)).

blocks.title: Book correction
blocks.text: The printed Figure 14.9(b) shows the velocity rising first (v = +x₀ω sin ωt). For x = x₀ cos ωt the velocity is v = −x₀ω sin ωt, so it falls first, as drawn above.
(iii) The acceleration of the particle executing SHM is given by the expression:
Putting x = x₀ cos ωt, we have:
The acceleration will be maximum (i.e., x₀ω²) at the extreme positions, and zero at the mean position.

blocks.alt: Graph of acceleration against time over one period, between omega squared xo and minus omega squared xo. The curve starts at its most negative value, rises through zero to its maximum at half a period and falls back: always opposite to the displacement.
blocks.caption: Figure 14.9 (c): Graphical representation of acceleration of oscillation performing S.H.M (original drawing after the textbook's Figure 14.9 (c)).

blocks.text: From the graph of Eqs. (14.19), (14.20) and (14.21) shown in Figs. 14.9 (a, b and c) can be seen that:

items: The phase difference between velocity and displacement is π/2.
The phase difference between acceleration and displacement is π/2.

blocks.title: Book correction
blocks.text: Since a = −ω²x, acceleration and displacement are always opposite: their phase difference is π, not π/2. Velocity differs from each of them by π/2.
However, it must be noted that the phase difference between displacement, velocity and acceleration is π/2.
